name: PowerView - Find Foreign Group Members (Cross-Forest)
description: Enumerates users from one domain who are members of groups in another domain across a forest trust. Foreign domain users in local groups inherit those group's permissions — sometimes including high-privilege access. Essential for finding cross-forest privilege escalation paths that aren't obvious from single-domain enumeration.
source: CPTS Module 13: Active Directory Enumeration & Attacks
notes:
=== WHAT THIS FINDS ===
When organizations merge or establish forest trusts, accounts from Forest A
may be added to groups in Forest B. This card finds those accounts:
  'User INLANEFREIGHT\admin is member of FREIGHTLOGISTICS\Administrators'

This means INLANEFREIGHT\admin has administrator rights in FREIGHTLOGISTICS.
If you compromised admin in INLANEFREIGHT → you have admin in FREIGHTLOGISTICS too.

=== OUTPUT COLUMNS ===
  GroupDomain      → which domain the group is in
  GroupName        → group name
  GroupDistinguishedName → full DN of the group
  MemberDomain     → which domain the member is FROM (the foreign account)
  MemberName       → SID of the foreign member (run Convert-SidToName to get readable name)
  MemberDistinguishedName → full DN of the member

=== CONVERTING SID TO NAME ===
The output often shows SIDs instead of names for foreign accounts:
  Convert-SidToName S-1-5-21-...-1170
  or: Get-DomainUser -Identity S-1-5-21-...-1170

=== REAL-WORLD SCENARIO ===
FreightLogistics trust: INLANEFREIGHT.LOCAL ↔ FREIGHTLOGISTICS.LOCAL
Get-DomainForeignGroupMember -Domain FREIGHTLOGISTICS.LOCAL finds:
  INLANEFREIGHT\administrator = member of FREIGHTLOGISTICS\Administrators
Result: INLANEFREIGHT admin creds give admin rights in FREIGHTLOGISTICS
→ Evil-WinRM to FREIGHTLOGISTICS DC with INLANEFREIGHT admin creds

=== ALSO CHECK BIDIRECTIONAL ===
Get-DomainForeignGroupMember -Domain INLANEFREIGHT.LOCAL
→ Finds FREIGHTLOGISTICS users who have rights in INLANEFREIGHT

examples.label: Find foreign members in foreign domain groups

references.title: HTB Academy - Active Directory Enumeration & Attacks

recommended.note: Leverage trust data for cross-domain forging.

defense.why_it_works: Get-DomainForeignGroupMember queries the AD group membership objects in the target domain using LDAP, filtering for members whose SID domain prefix differs from the group's domain. This is a native AD query — any authenticated domain user can enumerate group memberships across trusts because group objects and their members are accessible to all authenticated users by default.
defense.prerequisites: PowerShell with PowerView loaded. Any valid domain credential with trust access to the target domain. Domain-joined host or runas /netonly session.
defense.impact: Reveals cross-domain/cross-forest privilege paths that may not be apparent from single-domain enumeration. Finding a foreign account in a high-privilege group (Administrators, Domain Admins) in another domain means existing credentials from a compromised domain immediately grant access to another — no additional exploitation required.
defense.detection: PowerShell Script Block Logging (Event 4104) if enabled will log PowerView function calls including Get-DomainForeignGroupMember. LDAP query traffic to the foreign domain's DC on port 389/636. AMSI detection of PowerView strings if not obfuscated. EDR telemetry on PowerShell loading PowerView module.
defense.prevention: Enable PowerShell Script Block Logging and constrained language mode. AMSI and EDR with PowerView detection rules. Limit cross-domain group memberships — audit regularly and remove unnecessary foreign group members (Get-ADGroupMember for privileged groups). JEA to restrict what PowerShell can enumerate. Consider using protected users or tiered admin model to prevent foreign accounts from gaining local admin.
defense.evasion: Obfuscate PowerView function names. Use direct LDAP queries via .NET System.DirectoryServices instead of PowerView. Target only specific groups rather than full enumeration. Spread queries over time. Use Get-ADGroupMember (signed AD module) instead of PowerView to avoid detection signatures.
defense.misconfiguration: Domain trusts (especially bidirectional and forest trusts) extend authentication boundaries. SID filtering is often disabled on forest trusts to support legacy applications — but this allows an attacker with Domain Admin in a child domain to forge a golden ticket with ExtraSids claiming Domain Admin SID in the parent/trusted forest. Without SID filtering (SIDHistory filtering), domain boundaries offer no security isolation.
defense.vulnerable_config:
# Bidirectional forest trust without SID filtering:
Get-ADTrust -Filter * | Select-Object Name, Direction, SIDFilteringQuarantined
# SIDFilteringQuarantined: False  <-- SID filtering DISABLED
# Direction: BiDirectional        <-- both domains trust each other

# Child domain to parent: SID filtering is always disabled by default
# Enterprise Admin SID (S-1-5-21-<root>-519) can be added to ExtraSids
# Golden ticket with ExtraSids = cross-domain privilege escalation
defense.secure_config:
# Enable SID filtering on external/forest trusts:
netdom trust <TrustingDomain> /domain:<TrustedDomain> /quarantine:yes
# 'Quarantine' = SID filtering enabled — ExtraSids from other domain are stripped

# For child-to-parent trusts (SID filtering can't be enabled without breaking functionality):
# Use Selective Authentication instead of full trust
# Only accounts explicitly granted 'Allowed to Authenticate' can use the trust
netdom trust <ParentDomain> /domain:<ChildDomain> /SelectiveAuth:yes

# Restrict SIDHistory (prevents ExtraSids abuse):
# Audit accounts with SIDHistory:
Get-ADUser -Filter {SIDHistory -like '*'} -Properties SIDHistory

# Monitor cross-forest authentication:
# Event 4769 on parent DC with ticket from child domain user
